paras: The lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others took place on the night of Thursday, May 17, 1888, when a party of vigilantes hanged four men accused of horse stealing in No Man's Land, near Woodward, Indian Territory. Two of the dead were described as known outlaws, while the other two were strangers who protested their innocence to the end. The story ran nationally as a wire item, and one dispatch stated that there was 'no reasonable certainty' that the two strangers were guilty.

According to the dispatches, one of the men belonged to the 'notorious Chitwood boys', who were accused of robbing, thieving and murdering for years in the neutral strip and in southern Kansas. Another, known as 'Dandy' Hook, was said to have 'a score of aliases' and to be wanted by Kansas authorities, who had offered rewards for him.

On Thursday night a party of vigilantes overtook and captured four men driving a herd of stolen ponies in No Man's Land. Two of the captives said they had only been hired to help care for the horses and that they had come by them honestly. In the wire's words their story 'was hooted', and all four were 'promptly lynched'. The second dispatch placed the hanging near the western border of the Cherokee strip and said all were hanged 'on the charge of horse-stealing'.

Chitwood's brothers, described as members of a band of outlaws, declared that they would not leave the country until they had avenged his death. The vigilantes in turn warned them to leave at once. The coverage contains no report of an inquest, arrests or any official response, and neither of the two strangers was ever named.

Coverage came from two separate dispatches datelined Woodward. The first was printed from Texas to New York between May 19 and May 26, under headlines such as 'Horse Thieves Promptly Lynched' in the San Antonio Daily Light, 'Four Men Lynched by Vigilantes' in the New York Sun, and 'Horse Thieves Hung!' in the Emporia Weekly News. Most versions repeated its remark that Chitwood and Hook 'perhaps deserved their fate', though the Sun and the Press and Daily Dakotaian left it out. Shorter versions ran in the Salt Lake Herald, the Elko Daily Independent and the Daily Kennebec Journal.

The second dispatch, carried by the Springfield Daily Republic and the Griggs Courier, likened the Chitwood boys to 'the Benders' but also raised doubt about the two strangers' guilt. Weekly news summaries condensed it into a one-sentence item dated 'the 18th', which said all four were 'charged with robbery, thievery and murder'. That item appeared in small papers in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin and Dakota. The Western Kansas World headed the story 'No man's Land Law.', and at year's end the True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, included the four under May 17 in its list of 'Victims of Judge Lynch'. None of the reports stated the race of the victims.

Both Woodward dispatches put the lynching on Thursday night, and the year-end list gives May 17. The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer instead said 'on Friday', and the weekly summaries gave 'the 18th'; these were condensed columns printed later. Spellings of the names also varied, with Chitwood given as Chetwood or Chetewood and Hook as 'Danderhook' or 'Dandhook'.

reader.title: Lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others
bases: Two Woodward dispatches say a party of vigilantes captured four men with stolen horses and lynched or hanged all four (A2, A8, A20).

A 'party of vigilantes', not officers, captured four men and hanged them 'on the charge of horse-stealing' without trial (A2, A4, A8, A20); no headcount is given, but a party that overtook and hanged four men implies three or more.

Two differently worded dispatches from Woodward, I. T. (A2 and A8/A20) agree that vigilantes hanged four men, two of them named Chitwood and Dandy Hook, and a year-end list repeats it (A24); no report from a local Indian Territory paper was found.

accounts.label: First Woodward wire (May 19)
accounts.gist: Vigilantes overtook four men driving stolen ponies in No Man's Land Thursday night; two noted criminals 'perhaps deserved their fate', the other two said they were hired hands, were not believed, and all four were lynched.

accounts.label: Second Woodward dispatch
accounts.gist: Four men were lynched near the western border of the Cherokee strip; one was a Chitwood brother, one 'Dandy' Hook; the two strangers protested innocence and there was 'no reasonable certainty' of their guilt; all were hanged for horse-stealing.
